questions.question: Merge sort's worst-case comparisons satisfy M(n) = 2M(n/2) + (n − 1). Where does the (n − 1) come from?
options: The two recursive calls on halves
Choosing the smallest element of the whole list
Merging two sorted halves of total size n
questions.explanation: Merging compares only the two front items each round, and in the worst case needs one comparison per element except the last: n − 1.

questions.question: Why does Towers of Hanoi need 2ⁿ − 1 moves while merge sort needs only about n log n comparisons?
options: Hanoi subproblems shrink by 1, so the recursion tree is n levels deep; merge sort halves, so it is only log n deep
Hanoi makes more recursive calls per step than merge sort
Merge sort does no work outside its recursive calls
questions.explanation: Both make two recursive calls. The difference is how fast the size shrinks: subtracting 1 gives a deep tree with exponentially many nodes, halving gives a shallow one.

questions.question: While using plug and chug on M(n), you get (n − 1) + (n − 2) + 4M(n/4). Why is it wise NOT to rewrite this as 2n − 3 + 4M(n/4)?
options: Keeping each level's term separate makes the pattern (n − 2ⁱ) easier to spot
The master theorem requires unsimplified terms
Simplifying would change the base case
questions.explanation: Both forms are equal, but separate terms reveal the structure n − 1, n − 2, n − 4, … which leads straight to the closed form.

questions.question: For T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n, what does the master theorem give?
questions.explanation: Here n^(log₂4) = n², and f(n) = n is smaller, so the leaves win (case 1) and T(n) = Θ(n²).
